paras: The killing of Joseph Williams took place at Marshalltown, Iowa, on the evening of August 27, 1900, when a Black drayman was shot to death by one of a party of drinking tramps after a quarrel over two young white girls. Wire reports presented Williams as a man killed for defending the girls and said Black residents were talking of lynching the killers. Two tramps, John Gray and Pat Dunn, were indicted for murder.

Williams, 49, had lived in Marshalltown for ten years, drove a single-horse dray, and had a wife and six children. The vacant ground near the stock yards, the local paper later complained, had been a gathering place for drinking tramps all summer.

About 6 o'clock Williams was walking home past the Northwestern stock yards when he saw two young cannery huskers, Rosa Buhrer and Mary Khile, crying among eight or ten tramps gathered around a keg of beer. He and another drayman, James Clem, got the girls past the gang; Clem then went to telephone the police, and Williams went home for a revolver. When he returned the quarrel was renewed, and according to the first local account his revolver was taken from his pocket and turned on him.

Cannery workers saw him run with four men behind him; he tripped, begged the leader not to shoot, and was hit over the right kidney. He reached the cannery office, said the tramps had insulted two little girls and he had taken it up for them, and died within about fifteen minutes. Sheriff Shoemaker's posse and the police arrested thirty-five tramps and strangers that night, among them a man calling himself Gray. According to the Times-Republican, forty Black men "organized and assisted in the search during the night."

At the coroner's inquest on August 29 most witnesses named Gray as the man who fired, while his companion Pat Dunn gave conflicting testimony blaming an unknown man. The jury sealed its verdict, in part because of "quiet threats that are being made to lynch the murderer." Charged on informations signed by the widow, Gray and Dunn were held without bail, and Williams' two teenage sons picked Gray out at the jail.
The grand jury indicted both men for murder on September 15, and on September 27 their cases were continued to the next term. No report of a trial was found, and no lynching was attempted.

A brief Marshalltown wire told of four tramps who insulted two girls and an "old negro drayman" shot when he went to their rescue. Its headlines made the case a story of racial heroism, from the St. Louis Republic's "GIRLS' PROTECTOR KILLED" to "HEROISM IN HUMBLE GARB" in small weeklies and the Scranton Tribune's "HIS SKIN BLACK; HIS HEART WHITE." A Washington version said Black residents had set out "vowing to lynch" the tramps and that the sheriff's posse was sent partly to protect them.

The Marshalltown Times-Republican wrote that Williams had "reversed the usual order of things" by dying for two white girls. Yet the same issue printed the girls' statement that two colored girls had abused them and the tramps had taken their part, and concluded that Williams "misunderstood the situation." Afterward the paper used the case to argue for curbing liquor sales to tramps, warning that another such crime "might make a lynching impossible to prevent."

In the Black press the Indianapolis Recorder reprinted the first wire as "DANGEROUS TRAMPS," and the Iowa State Bystander ran a wire item saying violence was not expected despite intense excitement "among the negroes." A Bystander correspondent called the killing one of the saddest events in Marshalltown and wrote that "every colored man ought to take a hand and see that none of the hobos light here."

An Oskaloosa dispatch said Williams was simply passing three tramps and mentioned no girls. The physician's testimony that the fatal bullet was center-fire, unlike the rim-fire cartridges in Williams' home, cast doubt on the report that he was shot with his own revolver. Six witnesses picked Gray as the shooter and two picked Dunn, while the first wire said two tramps fired.

reader.title: Killing of Joseph Williams
bases: Joseph Williams, a Black drayman, was shot by one of a group of drinking tramps after a quarrel over two girls; no paper gives a racial motive, the killers were not a lynch mob, and the only lynching talk was of Black residents and others against the accused tramps (A4, A6, A11, A2).

The local Marshalltown paper, independent wire dispatches and two Black papers agree that tramps shot Williams to death near the canning factory on the evening of Aug. 27 (A4, A1, A12, A14), though they differ on how the quarrel began (A2, A7, A12).

accounts.gist: Four tramps insulted two girls, Williams went to their rescue and two of the tramps shot him; the Black population was aroused and the killers might be lynched.

accounts.label: Local paper, first day
accounts.gist: Williams and James Clem got the girls past a drinking gang; Williams went home for a revolver, returned, was disarmed in a renewed quarrel and shot with his own gun as he fled.

accounts.label: The two girls
accounts.gist: Two colored girls had abused them and slapped one; the tramps took their part; Williams misunderstood and believed the tramps had insulted them.

accounts.label: Oskaloosa dispatch
accounts.gist: Three drunken tramps held Williams, who was passing them on his way home, and shot him in the back; no girls are mentioned.

accounts.label: Pat Dunn
accounts.gist: Dunn testified he was too drunk to take part and that the shooter was an unknown man who left on a freight for Tama, not Gray.

accounts.label: Black correspondent
accounts.gist: No one knew the facts, but everyone said Williams was protecting white girls the 'hobos' had insulted and was shot in the back while running away.

framing.detail: Wire headlines praised Williams as a protector of white girls ('GIRLS' PROTECTOR KILLED', 'HIS SKIN BLACK; HIS HEART WHITE') and called the killing wanton murder by tramps.

The local Times-Republican called Williams 'highly respected' and the crime 'foul', but printed the girls' story that he 'misunderstood the situation' and used the case to attack tramps and liquor sales.
Smaller papers ran the first wire under 'HEROISM IN HUMBLE GARB' or 'Shot and Killed by Tramps'.
The Indianapolis Recorder and the Iowa State Bystander ran the wire under 'DANGEROUS TRAMPS' and 'Murderer Identified'.
A Bystander correspondent called it one of the saddest events in Marshalltown and urged every Black man to see that no tramps settled there.
